planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or transplant divisions in spring, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Strawberry Seduction opens vivid cherry-red and fades gracefully through pink to cream as flowers age.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; like other yarrows, it will not tolerate heavy clay or consistently wet soil, especially through humid summers. Strawberry Seduction opens a vivid, saturated cherry-red and gradually fades through rose-pink to soft cream as each flat-topped flower cluster ages, so a single plant displays several colors simultaneously atop finely cut, aromatic, gray-green ferny foliage. It blooms from late spring through summer, and deadheading spent flower stems encourages continued flowering and a tidier appearance. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it performs best in lean, sharply drained soil where richer perennials would struggle, and dividing congested clumps every two to three years in spring keeps the plant vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Fireland Yarrow (Orange-Red Fading to Gold Yarrow)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Fireland opens fiery orange-red and ages through gold, giving a warm multicolor display on the same plant.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; excellent drainage matters more than fertility, since rich, wet soil leads to weak, floppy growth and crown rot. Fireland produces flat-topped clusters of flowers that open a vivid orange-red and age gracefully through amber to gold, giving a warm, multicolor tapestry effect across the plant as older and newer flowers open at different stages, held on sturdy stems above aromatic, finely cut gray-green foliage. It blooms from early summer into fall, especially with regular deadheading of spent flower heads, and its strong stems resist the flopping that troubles some taller yarrow cultivars. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it thrives in lean, sharply drained soil and benefits from division every two to three years in spring to maintain vigorous, dense growth.

common_name: Summer Pastels Yarrow (Mixed Soft-Color Seed Strain)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow after frost danger has passed, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Summer Pastels is a classic All-America Selections-winning mixed-color seed strain.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since yarrow rots readily in heavy, wet soil. Summer Pastels is a classic All-America Selections-winning seed strain producing a soft mix of cream, apricot, salmon, pink, and lavender flowers across a planting, a gentler palette than the bright golds and reds of many named yarrow cultivars, held on sturdy stems above aromatic, finely cut gray-green foliage from early summer through fall. Deadheading spent flower clusters extends the bloom season and keeps the planting tidy. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it performs best in lean, sharply drained soil, and because it is seed-grown, individual plants within a planting will vary somewhat in exact color, adding to its informal, cottage-garden charm.

common_name: Peach Seduction Yarrow (Soft Peach-Pink Fading Yarrow)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or transplant divisions in spring, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Peach Seduction is part of the Seduction series bred for compact habit and a long color-fade sequence.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; excellent drainage matters more than soil fertility, since wet, rich soil produces weak growth and invites crown rot. Peach Seduction opens a warm, soft peach-pink and gradually fades to a pale cream as each flower cluster ages, giving a gentle multicolor effect across the compact plant, held above aromatic, finely cut gray-green foliage from late spring through summer. Its more compact habit than older, taller yarrow cultivars fits smaller borders and mixed containers without staking. Deadhead spent flower clusters to prolong bloom, and expect exceptional drought and heat tolerance once established; divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigorous, floriferous growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Walther Funcke holds an intense brick orange-red color longer than many warm-colored yarrow cultivars before fading.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential, as this drought-loving perennial declines quickly in heavy, wet soil. Walther Funcke bears intensely colored, brick orange-red flower clusters that hold their saturated color longer into the season than many similarly toned yarrow cultivars before gradually softening toward copper and gold, set above finely cut, gray-green aromatic foliage from early summer into fall. Its rich, warm color pairs especially well with blue salvias, catmints, and ornamental grasses in a sunny mixed border. Deadhead spent flower heads to encourage continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous, since older yarrow clumps can become woody and open in the center.
